           The Roses are the stewards of a 140-year-old working cattle ranch, the Taylor-

Rose Ranch, that is bisected by the proposed Link G6.             The entirety of Taylor-Rose

Ranch, as discussed in detail below, is a recorded cultural resource.            As the Roses

testified, Link G6 would disrupt or make impossible some of its ranching activities.1        As

the Roses also testified, the centerline of Link G6 lies just 375 feet from the Roses’

historic restored 1904 home, so the Roses will be assaulted all day, every day, by the

line’s noise, vibrations, and electromagnetic fields, and it will dominate their landscape,

as well.2

I.        The Roses, like many intervenors in this proceeding, do not believe the
          proposed 765-kV line is necessary.

          The PUC approved the building of the three import lines as part of the Permian

Basin Reliability Plan in 2024, in proceedings in which few stakeholders participated.        It

acted under a legislative directive to include all prospective large power users in a

demand projection for the purposes of planning transmission lines.         But the inclusion of

prospective users that would each draw more power than many small cities quickly

skewed the numbers.             Therefore, in 2025, the Legislature passed S.B. 6, in order to

eliminate speculative requests by large load customers—i.e., data centers and crypto

miners.       Although the PUC had adjusted the raw demand numbers when approving the

Permian Basin Reliability Plan, it still likely includes speculative loads, the cost of which

should be paid by the speculators, not Texas consumers.         It also includes load that could

kV lines impose costs of up to $100 billion in lifetime costs, while not adding new

ERCOT generating capacity.4

II.      The Roses, like many intervenors in this proceeding, do not believe that the
         proposed 765-kV line is safe, particularly when their home is within 375 feet
         of the line that would bisect their working cattle ranch.

         A.      Link G6 runs perilously close to the Roses’ home.

         The historically and culturally significant Taylor-Rose Ranch is on Link G6.                        The

Roses’ home is only 375 feet away from the 765-kV line that would bisect their working

ranch.    The Roses would be exposed to the noise, vibrations, and electromagnetic field

from the transmission line 24/7/365.               They could not avoid it while they work their

cattle or tend to their pastures.         They could not avoid it even as they eat or sleep—nor

could their cattle or the many animals, birds, fish, and fowl on their property.

         B.      Dr. Gelmann’s cabined and dismissive testimony cannot guide the PUC
                 in its determination regarding prudent avoidance.

         Applicants did not address most medical issues raised.                        Applicants’ medical

expert, Dr. Gelmann, is not an epidemiologist—nor, as Mr. Bayliff elicited, a biophysicist,

neurologist, cardiologist, or electrophysiologist.5              He is an oncologist who specializes in

two things: prostate cancer6 and, since at least 2005—some twenty-one years—testifying

the John Norton Endowed Chair for Prostate Cancer Research at the University of

Arizona.8      His curriculum vitae mentions prostate cancer 133 times, electromagnetic

fields (“EMF”) not once.            One would think, if the science of EMF is as settled as Dr.

Gelmann testifies, that transmission line companies could find a variety of

epidemiologists, oncologists, biophysicists, neurologists, cardiologists and other medical

professionals with relevant training to testify.

        Dr. Gelmann, as he has for twenty-one years, relies primarily on a 2002 report for

his conclusions.9       That report, attached to his current testimony and referenced in all his

testimony since 2005—is Electric and Magnetic Fields Associated with the Use of

Electric Power (“EMF Report”), which was a survey of studies to that time.                                    Dr.

Gelmann has never deigned to look further.                  Science has moved on; Dr. Gelmann has

not.

        Yet when questioned even about the content of his 2002 EMF Report, Dr.

Gelmann dismissed the report’s inclusion of a Swedish study that found an association

between EMF exposure and an increased risk of chronic lymphocytic leukemia.10                                  Dr.

Gelmann was dismissive about the EMF Report’s conclusion that there was evidence,

“there were reports that go either way.”11               The same is true of the EMF Report’s

discussion regarding EMF exposure and increased risk of childhood leukemia.12                         None

of the studies were conclusive, Dr. Gelmann testified, as he also testified conclusively

that EMF did not cause cancer.13            Dr. Gelmann also refused to definitively recognize

that the EMF Report acknowledges that EMF could interfere with pacemakers and

defibrillators, stating only that, “It may,” showing surprising unfamiliarity with a

document he has cited since 2005.14            He continued: “Again, that is certainly outside my

expertise as I’m not, you know, an engineer or a technician for these items.”15                     He did

not address the additive effects of EMF from a transmission line: while he did briefly

mention the predicted amount of EMF in the right-of-way,16 he did not mention that it is

cumulative of any other source of EMF, including farm equipment.

        Further, many of the additional studies that Dr. Gelmann cites as references (and

none of which he, whose specialty is prostate cancer, authored) are also dated, some

going as far back as far as thirty-eight years.17          Of forty-three cited publications, fifteen

were published between 1988 and 1999, twenty-four were published between 2000 and

         Importantly, Dr. Gelmann also admitted that he is not an expert in the siting of

transmission lines and expressed no opinion how far homes or other structures should be

from transmission lines for safety purposes.20                  He could not say whether 500 feet, 1,000

feet, or some other distance is the safest distance from a transmission line and a home.21

        C.       Should the PUC grant the Application, it should require Applicants to
                 adjust for the unknown and move the 765-kV line as far from
                 habitations as possible.

        Should the PUC grant the Application, the PUC’s policy of prudent avoidance

should require that Applicants generously adjust for those unknowns.                        In the Roses’ case,

a 765-kV transmission line that lies within 375 feet of their home and that bisects a

working ranch in a way that makes avoidance of it impossible, for every hour of every

day, is unacceptable.

III.    Should the PUC grant the Application, Save the Lampasas’ Routes 572, 296
        and 295 are inferior to Routes 894 and 487.
        Should the PUC grant the Application, Save the Lampasas’ preferred routes are inferior to

Routes 894 and 487.         All three of Save the Lampasas’ initially supported routes—Routes 572,

296 and 295—use Link G6, which includes the historically significant Taylor-Rose Ranch.                        The

Taylor-Rose Ranch is a recorded historical and cultural resource.

        A.       Save the Lampasas asserts that Applicants could avoid the trinomial on
                 the Taylor-Rose Ranch but the entirety of the Taylor-Rose Ranch is
                 within that trinomial’s boundaries—and its 7,224 foot length cannot be
                 spanned.

        Save the Lampasas states in its initial brief that a historic heritage ranch need not

be completely avoided but that siting professional will seek to suggest a route that avoids

Reinecke, for the proposition that eligible trinomials can be crossed by development if it

would not be detrimental to the eligibility of that trinomial.25          While that might be true

in general, there is a difference between a property that may have a trinomial-eligible

resource that is located somewhere within its property lines, on one hand, and a

property—such as the Taylor-Rose Ranch—that is completely within the boundaries of a

trinomial, on the other.

        Certainly, in the ordinary case, a utility may be able to span over, say, a scattering

of arrowheads, or a cave, or other culturally important resource.              Applicants testified

that if significant archeological sites are identified during the field investigation,

Applicants will work with the THC to “shift structure locations along the route alignment

to span the site, thereby avoiding the placement of foundations within recorded site

boundaries.”26       Here, the recorded site boundaries of Trinomial No. 41BT562 are the

entirety of the Taylor-Rose Ranch,27 which runs for 7,224 feet.28             It is not possible for

Applicants to span 7,224 feet.          Applicants testified that the 765-kV steel lattice tower

that will primarily be used for the Proposed Transmission Line Project “generally allows

for a typical span length of approximately 1,400–1,500 feet.”29           Applicants’ witness, Ms.

Cooley, further testified that, “The maximum span that we anticipate would probably be

Taylor-Rose Ranch is not a possibility.

        B.       Other issues with Routes 572, 296, and 295 militate against their
                 adoption.

        Route 572.        Link J31 remains a problem.             The possibility of interfering with

cathodic protection is real, which is why the PUC changed its rule regarding the

paralleling of pipelines.       Call it prudent location: why would one possibly degrade crude

oil, natural gas, and highly volatile liquids pipelines, as those pipelines traverse the

Colorado River?31         Additionally, the Colorado River Alliance Intervenors32 testified

extensively that the use of Link J31 would result in the fragmentation of dedicated

golden-cheeked warbler habitat.

        Route 296.       Route 296 also contains Link F34, as well as Link G6.                      Save the

Lampasas suggests that the transmission line could be moved to avoid the 500-child

elementary school that now exists on Link F34, in Florence Independent School

District.33    But the map shows little room to maneuver, without moving too close to

adjoining properties that did not receive notice.                    More importantly, the Florence

Independent School District, which believes the school will grow to 740 students, does

not think that is a possibility. 34          Also, PUC witness Mr. Poole testified on cross-

examination that the presence of the school was an issue and other routes should be

IV.       Should the PUC grant the Application, Cherokee Creek’s CCG route is
          inferior to Routes 894 and 487.

          A.       Cherokee Creek, espousing Route CCG, misstates by 50% the number
                   of recorded cultural resources that Route CCG crosses and wrongly
                   concludes Route CCG performs on par with Routes 894 and 487.

          The Cherokee Creek Aligned Intervenors (“Cherokee Creek”) espouse Route CCG,

which also includes Link G6.                In their Initial Post-Hearing Brief, Cherokee Creek states

that “Route CCG, Route 894, and Route 487 are all identical, each crossing two recorded

cultural resource sites and ranking within the second quartile of all filed routes.”38           This

is wrong.        Although it is true that Applicants’ original EA, Table 7-3 showed no

recorded cultural resources on Link G6—a link Route CCG uses—evidence adduced at

hearing showed that both Applicants’ original EA, and its updated Exhibit 23, failed to

include the known, recorded cultural resource on Link G6, Trinomial No. 41BT562.39

recorded cultural resources, and that the single metric favoring Route 894 and 487 is one

           B.       That Cherokee Creek ignores the Taylor-Rose Ranch does not change
                    the fact that the entire ranch is within Trinomial No. 41BT562 and
                    cannot be spanned.

           Save the Lampasas cites Cherokee Creek’s expert, Ms. Reinecke, on the effect of a

trinomial. Cherokee Creek, since it does not mention the Taylor-Rose Ranch at all, does

not. But the same analysis applies: the entirety of the Taylor-Rose Ranch—its 7,224 foot

length—is within the boundaries of the trinomial and cannot be spanned.

           C.       Other issues with Route CCG militates against its adoption.

           Other issues with Route CCG militates against its adoption:46

           • Route CCG is 9 miles longer than Route 894 and 10.69 miles longer than Route

                487.

           • Route CCG crosses a significantly greater number of streams than Route 894 or

                Route 487: Route CCG crosses 346 streams compared to Route 894, which

                crosses 291, and Route 487, which crosses 282.

           • Route CCG has 105 habitable structures within 500 feet of the centerline,

                compared to Route 894, which has 85, and Route 487, which has 96.

historical and cultural site the entirety of which is within the boundaries of Trinomial No.
